{{short description|Russian conservationist and zoologist}}
'''Vladimir Evgenievich Flint''' (Владимир Евгеньевич Флинт; March 14, 1924 – March 23, 2004) was a Russian conservationist and zoologist, specializing in ornithology.<ref>Памяти Владимира Евгеньевича Флинта (14 марта 1924 — 23 марта 2004) // Мир птиц. август 2003—июнь 2004. № 3-1 (№ 27-28). С. 1. (In memory of Vladimir Evgenievich Flint (March 14, 1924 – March 23, 2004) // The World of Birds. August 2003–June 2004, No. 3-1, pages 27-28)</ref> He was the author or co-author of more than 650 papers and books dealing with zoology and wildlife conservation.<ref name=Ibis>{{cite journal|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1474-919X.2006.00502.x |doi=10.1111/j.1474-919X.2006.00502.x |title=Professor Vladimir E. Flint (1924–2004) |date=2006 |last1=Kurochkin |first1=Evgeny |last2=Galushin |first2=Vladimir |last3=Lebedeva |first3=Elena |journal=Ibis |volume=148 |pages=193–194 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Biography==
Vladimir E. Flint was born in Moscow and grew up in the neighborhood of [[Bolshaya Ordynka Street]]. From childhood, he took a serious interest in birds.<ref name=Sapsan>{{Cite web|url=https://sapsan-fond.ru/en/vladimir-evgenievich-flint/|title=Vladimir Evgenievich Flint – Sapsan Foundation}}</ref> His father, E. E. Flint (1887–1975), was a professor of crystallography. In WW II Vladimir Flint served in combat as a crew member of a [[T-34]] and became [[shell-shocked]], but returned to the front. He ended the war on the [[Elbe]] with the rank of senior lieutenant, acting as second in command to the officer commanding a machine gun platoon.<ref name=anniversary>Владимир Евгеньевич Флинт (к 60-летию со дня рождения) // «Охота и охотничье хозяйство», № 3, 1984. стp.20-21 (Vladimir Evgenievich Flint (on the 60th anniversary of his birth) // “Hunting and hunting economy”, No. 3, 1984. pp. 20-21)</ref>

After military service from 1942 to the spring of 1946, Flint worked in Moscow for two years and took academic classes in the evenings. In 1948 he entered the Biological Faculty of [[Moscow State University]] (MSU). In 1953 Vladimir graduated from MSU University with a diploma thesis on the [[eider]] of the White Sea's [[Onega Bay]].<ref name=anniversary/> After graduation, he entered a postgraduate course in the [[Gamaleya Research Institute of Epidemiology and Microbiology]]. There he did research on rodents and spatial clusters of rodent-borne epidemics.<ref name=Ibis/> In 1959 he defended his [[Candidate of Sciences|candidate]]'s dissertation<ref name=anniversary/> "On the zoological foundatoins of epidemiological exploration".<ref name=Sapsan/> From 1969 to 1976 he was a senior research fellow at the Zoological Museum of Moscow State University. In 1972 he defended his [[Doctor of Sciences|Russian doctoral]] dissertation<ref name=anniversary/> on "The spatial structure of populations of small mammals".<ref name=Sapsan/> In 1976 he became the head of the department of wildlife protection at the All-Russian Research Institute for Nature Conservation of the State Committee on Ecology of Russia (formerly the Central Laboratory for Nature Conservation of the USSR Ministry of Agriculture).<ref name=anniversary/> He worked at the institute for the remainder of his career.<ref name=Ibis/>

V. E. Flint published not only scientific monographs and articles, field guides, and textbooks for universities, but also many popular science essays and children's books. He was a frequent guest on the popular Russian television show «В мире животных» ([[In the World of Animals]]).<ref name=anniversary/>

He died in Moscow on March 23, 2004. The urn with his ashes is in a family grave in section 4 of the [[Donskoye Cemetery]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.moscow-tombs.ru/2004/flint_ve.htm |title=Могила В. Е. Флинта (V. E. Flint's Grave) |archive-date=2017-06-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170602001759/http://www.moscow-tombs.ru/2004/flint_ve.htm }}</ref>

==Contributions to nature conservation==
V. E. Flint was among the founders of the USSR Ornithological Society in 1983.<ref name=Ibis/> He was the leader for the creation in 1993 of the Союз охраны птиц России (abbreviated СОПР; Russian Bird Conservation Union). He was the union's president for almost 10 years and then became honorary president.<ref name=anniversary/>

Flint focused on the conservation and restoration of rare species of birds and mammals. He was a leader in the development of captive breeding centers for saving genetic resources and for the reintroduction and population restoration of threatened wildlife. Some on the animals benefitting from his work were [[Crane (bird)|crane]]s, [[Raptor (bird)|raptor]]s, [[great bustard]]s, and [[Mongolian gazelle]]s.<ref name=Ibis/>

In 1973 he became the first Russian scientist to make contact with the [[International Crane Foundation]]. He was the leader of the international "Project Sterkh", involving ornithologists who exported and imported hatching eggs of the [[Siberian crane]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=In Honor of Vladimir Flint|journal=The ICF Bugle: International Crane Foundation, Quarterly Newsletter|volume=30|issue=4|page=3|date=November 2004|url=https://savingcranes.org/wp-content/uploads/2008/05/2004v30n4.pdf}}</ref>

Vladimir Flint participated in the creation of the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]]'s [[IUCN Red List|Red Data Books]] and in the preparation of legislative acts on nature conservation. He was one of the authors and editors of the Red Data Book of the USSR (1978, 1982), the Red Data Book of the RSFSR (1983), the Red Data Book of the Russian Federation (2001) and the Red Data Book of Moscow (2001). He is the author of the draft of the USSR law «Об охране и использовании животного мира» ("On the Protection and Use of Wildlife"), which declared fundamentally new legal norms. The law was approved and put into effect by a decree of the [[Supreme Soviet]] of the USSR on January 1, 1981.<ref name=anniversary/> He also promoted international cooperation for wildlife conservation by facilitating visits by people like [[Gerald Durrell]] and Sir [[Peter Scott]] to remote areas of Russia.<ref name=Ibis/>

Flint was elected as a representative of the USSR to the Council and Bureau of the [[IUCN]], became vice-chairman of the IUCN Rare Species Commission, a member of the International Ornithological Committee and its Executive Committee, a member of the Scientific Council of the International Crane Conservation Fund, and national coordinator of Russia's cooperation with the International Bureau for the Study and Conservation of Wetlands.<ref name=anniversary/>

==Expeditions==
V. E. Flint visited more than 50 foreign countries. As a member of the board of the Ассоциации дружбы с народами Африки (Association of Friendship with the Peoples of Africa), V. E. Flint organized a number of trips to the national parks of [[Kenya]], [[Uganda]], and [[Tanzania]]. Together with such scientists as Andrei Grigorievich Bannikov, Yuri Andreevich Isakov, Viktor Alekseevich Popov (1910–1980), and others, he was among the first Soviet zoologists to see with their own eyes the animal world of the [[savannah]]s of [[East Africa]].<ref name=anniversary/>

Flint worked in expeditions in Northern [[Kazakhstan]], [[Primorsky Krai]], [[Tuva]], [[Transbaikalia]], [[Turkmenistan]] and other republics of Central Asia. Since 1963, his attention was drawn to the north — he visited the [[Barents Sea]]'s [[Murmansk]] coast, [[Wrangel Island]], the tundra of [[Yakutia]], and the [[Taimyr Peninsula]].<ref name=anniversary/> In all his expeditions, he took every opportunity to study birds.<ref name=Ibis/>

==Family==
V. E. Flint was married to Tatyana Lvovna Zenkevich (Muromtseva), a marine biologist and a daughter of Lev Aleksandrovich Zenkevich, an oceanographer. Their older son Mikhail Vladimirovich (born 1949), was a corresponding member of the Russian Academy of Sciences, head of the Laboratory of Ecology and Distribution of [[Plankton]], and deputy director of the P. P. Shirshov Institute of Oceanology of the Russian Academy of Sciences (Moscow).<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20131109094137/http://msk.rgo.ru/ob-otdelenii/uchyonyj-sovet-mc-rgo/flint-mixail-vladimirovich/ Флинт Михаил Владимирович (Flint Mikhail Vladimirovich), 2010, Русское географическое общество. Московское городское отделение. (Russian Geographical Society. Moscow City Branch)]</ref> The younger son Alexander (born 1953) was director of the St. Demetrius School of Sisters of Mercy (Moscow) from 1992 to 2003 and, subsequently, became general director of «Информационно-образовательный центр „Соучастие“», a non-profit organization for promoting information, education, and charitable participation, for the [[Russian Orthodox Church]].<ref>[http://www.ortho-rus.ru/cgi-bin/ps_file.cgi?5_1973 Флинт Александр Владимирович (Flint Alexander Vladimirovich)]; [http://www.ortho-rus.ru/cgi-bin/ps_file.cgi?5_1973 на сайте Благотворительного фонда «Русское Православие» (website of the Russian Orthodoxy Charitable Foundation)]</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Flint was elected a full member (academician) of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=Sapsan/> He was elected to honorary memberships in the [[British Ornithologists' Union]] (1985), the [[National Geographic Society]] (1989), and the [[British Trust for Ornithology]] (1992).<ref name=Ibis/>

Flint was awarded the [[Order of the Patriotic War]] 1st class. He was appointed Honored Ecologist of the Russian Federation.<ref name=anniversary/> He was awarded in 1981 the [[Order of Friendship of Peoples]] and in 1985 Holland's [[Order of the Golden Ark]]. In 1987 he received both the [[Audubon#Audubon Medal]] of the [[Audubon|National Audubon Society]] and the UNEP International Award "Global-500".<ref name=Ibis/>
